etymology: Old English clerc, a cleric - the literate man who kept the book because he was the one who could read.
office: The minutes, the roll, and the file that proves both.
tell: Knows the quorum rule without looking it up
Keeps the version that was actually adopted
keystone: Without the clerk there is no record, and without a record there is no way to prove what the body did - which is the first thing a Sabotriot needs and the last thing they check.

confused_with.tell: The clerk keeps what the body did this year; the archivist keeps what it did in 1974.

senses: The officer who keeps the body's memory: the agenda, the roll call, the minutes, the motions as adopted rather than as proposed. In most places this is an elected or appointed post with a statutory duty to the record.

It works because procedure is evidence. A vote nobody recorded is a vote somebody can deny, so the clerk's real power is not the gavel but the file - and the job stays invisible precisely until it is done badly.
example: *"Two years later the only proof of what the council had voted for was the **clerk**'s minutes, and the member who had denied it was reading them aloud."*
